newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Flat Swedish CPI not seen as ending inflation rise.
newsitem.headline: Flat Swedish CPI not seen as ending inflation rise.

text.p: Swedish debt yields fell on Tuesday morning after a lower than expected consumer price index showed prices unchanged in July from June but analysts still expected the rate of inflation to rise this autumn.
But analysts agreed that the figure for July would have a positive effect on the market.
"But the year-on-year inflation figure will rise on the ground of tax increases and not due to increased demand," said Peter Lindquist, economist at HSBC Midland.

The CPI showed unchanged prices between July and June for an year-on-year inflation rate of 1.0 percent. The market had expected to see a rise of 0.1 percent for the month for a year-on-year rise of 1.2 percent.

Statistics Sweden said seasonally lower prices for clothes and shoes largely offset a 0.4 percent rise in food prices and higher costs of housing. Lower costs for interest rates were also recorded in July.
By midday the 10 year bond yield was nine basis points lower at 6.54 percent and the six month T-bill rate two basis points lower at 4.33 percent.

"The figure was better than consensus. The market is going well, aided by positive sentiment in Germany where interest rates were left unchanged today," said James McKay, economist at U.S. investment bank PaineWebber.
"Inflation is continuing to be benign and I wonder if the Riksbank will raise rates if the Bundesbank does this autumn. There is a 50/50 chance."

On Tuesday the Riksbank left its key rate, the repo, unchanged at 4.10 percent at its weekly repurchase operation. The repo rate, its key tool for controlling money market liquidity, has been unchanged since December 17.

McKay said it all depended on how much the Swedish economy picked up speed over the rest of 1997 and if the inflation trend moved toward the Riksbank's goal of two percent, with a leeway of one percentage point in either direction.

Tomas Pousette, Nordbanken economist, said the belief that inflation would step up in the autumn had not disappeared even though today's figure was lower than expected and a positive boost for the market.
"The rate of inflation will rise because we have had low price pressure for 12 months and we have now reached the bottom for interest rates," Pousette said.
Swedbank had forecast no change for the month.
"But there was a risk on the upside with retail trade going so well," said Mikael Hindrika, Swedbank economist.
"The rate of inflation is expected to increase this autumn and Swedbank forecasts an annual average of 0.8 percent in 1998 and about two percent in 1998.
"But the figure today should have a positive effect because the market was expecting to see a higher number," he added.
